answer: I'd like to talk about something I brought back to life last year. Something I managed to repair myself was an old bicycle that had been sitting unused for years because of a series of faults. It was the bike I used to ride to school, and it had been gathering dust in a corner of our building's parking area ever since. The tyres were flat, the chain was rusted and the brakes barely worked. One of the pedals was also loose, so it made an awful clicking sound whenever anyone tried to ride it. Rather than throwing it away or paying for repairs, I decided to attempt to fix it myself, which was rather [[ambitious]] given my limited skills. I watched several tutorials, bought a few basic parts and set about it patiently over a weekend. I patched the inner tubes, scrubbed the rust off the chain and oiled it, then replaced the brake pads and tightened everything I could find. The bicycle mechanic near our local market kindly lent me a special tool when I got stuck. The process was more [[fiddly]] than I expected, and there were moments of real frustration. But gradually, piece by piece, the bicycle came back to life. When I finally took it for a ride along the river, the sense of [[accomplishment]] was genuinely satisfying. What pleased me most was that I had saved money and rescued something from the [[scrap heap]]. Honestly, repairing it myself was far more [[rewarding]] than simply buying a new one. It gave me a real appreciation for fixing things rather than discarding them.

followUps.q: Do you still ride the bicycle?
followUps.answer: Yes, mostly for short trips around town and for evening rides along the river. It's also a nice way to get some exercise without having to go to a gym.

followUps.q: Do you usually repair things or replace them?
followUps.answer: I try to repair them where possible. It's cheaper, less wasteful and more satisfying, although with modern electronics that's getting harder, because many simply aren't designed to be [[repairable]].
